summary:
Feynman's Legacy is a planetary-analog platform for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It identifies and ranks places on Earth that share environmental, geological and operational conditions with proposed permanent bases on the Moon and Mars.

Earth is covered by a global 0.5 degree grid of 85,726 locations across 92 months from 2019 to 2026, built from 12 MERRA-2 products, 4 MODIS Terra products, NASA SEDAC population data, NASA EONET natural events, Macrostrat lithology, ISRIC SoilGrids and SRTM, ETOPO1 and GMTED terrain. The Moon is covered by 60 equal-area regions built from 36 LRO, GRAIL, Lunar Prospector and SELENE datasets. Mars is covered by MOLA, TES, Odyssey GRS, CRISM and Mars 2020 CTX data.

Eight reference bases, two lunar and six Martian, are defined by 77 measured target values with source and confidence. A shared taxonomy of 21 niches and 51 criteria scores every location, with coverage-aware aggregation, clustering and a 500 kilometer separation rule. A logistics layer adds accessibility, support bases and routes, and LightGBM projects each score three months ahead.

The result is 358 analog pairs across 187 sites in 35 countries, each with a per-variable explanation, published through a read-only FastAPI service and an interactive Three.js globe.
details:
Feynman's Legacy: Terrestrial Analogs for Permanent Moon and Mars Bases

OVERVIEW

Feynman's Legacy is a planetary-analog platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It identifies and ranks places on Earth that share environmental, geological and operational conditions with proposed permanent bases on the Moon and Mars, and it explains each recommendation variable by variable.

The platform integrates three independent bodies of evidence. Earth is covered by a global 0.5 degree grid of 85,726 locations spanning 92 months from 2019 to 2026, enriched with terrain, soil, geology, land cover, population and natural-event layers. The Moon is covered by an equal-area scientific base built from 36 LRO, GRAIL, Lunar Prospector and SELENE datasets. Mars is covered by MOLA topography, TES thermal inertia, Odyssey elemental abundances and Jezero mineralogy at CTX resolution.

Against these datasets, the platform scores every terrestrial location against eight reference bases, two lunar and six Martian, whose target values come from published mission measurements rather than assumptions. Results are ranked, clustered, enriched with logistics, projected forward with machine learning, and served through a read-only API to an interactive 3D application.

THE PROBLEM

Site selection for the Moon and Mars is expensive to test in situ. Before hardware is committed, mission planners need terrestrial places where suits, habitats, drills, rovers, instruments and procedures can be validated under conditions that resemble the target environment.

Four difficulties make this hard. Datasets for three bodies differ in resolution, projection, units, variable definitions and time coverage, with no shared schema. Reference bases do not come with machine-readable environmental specifications, so those must be assembled from mission literature. Similarity alone is not enough, because a site can be an excellent physical match and still be unreachable or unsustainable to operate. And large homogeneous regions produce hundreds of near-identical candidates, which hides genuinely distinct options.

The challenge theme addressed is: identify Earth locations that analog the permanent Moon base locations and Mars.

OBJECTIVES AND SOLUTION

The objective is a reproducible ranking of terrestrial analog sites for proposed lunar and Martian bases, where every score can be traced to a source, a unit and a measurement.

The solution has six stages. Normalization maps all three bodies onto a shared taxonomy of 21 niches and 51 criteria, built from 34 distinct variables. Targets are taken from published measurements, each with source, unit and confidence level, and compared against terrestrial values using a tolerance derived from the Earth distribution. Scoring converts distance into a 0 to 100 scale and aggregates criteria by weight with coverage renormalization. Diversity is enforced by clustering and by a 500 kilometer separation rule. Logistics combines accessibility, support infrastructure and route availability. Machine learning projects how each pair's score evolves over the following three months.

Every recommendation carries a generated explanation describing which niches match, which differ and by how much, which data are missing, how good the logistics are and what the model expects next.

DATA SOURCES

Earth, global grid. 85,726 locations covering 92 months from January 2019 to August 2026, with 16 dynamic variables and 67 static attributes. Twelve monthly MERRA-2 products from NASA GIBS provide air temperature, precipitation, snowfall, evaporation, root-zone soil water, precipitable water vapour, incident shortwave radiation, surface albedo, wind speed, dust surface mass concentration, total dust deposition and aerosol optical depth. Four MODIS Terra products provide daytime and nighttime land surface temperature, NDVI and the 2024 IGBP land cover classification. The grid is complemented by NASA SEDAC GPW v4 2020 population density, NASA EONET v3 natural events covering fires, volcanic activity, severe storms, snow, extreme temperatures, landslides, floods, dust and haze, sea and lake ice and droughts, Macrostrat lithology and geologic units, ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0 soil properties, and AWS Terrain Tiles at zoom 6 derived from SRTM, ETOPO1 and GMTED for relief and slope. Four variables are derived in-project: solar geometry including sun height and 24-hour daylight days, ICAO standard-atmosphere pressure from altitude, MODIS day-night thermal amplitude, and a permafrost index from MERRA-2.

Earth, classical analog sites. Eight well-studied analog sites are maintained as a separate reference set: Atacama, Askja, Devon Island, Dry Valleys, Kilauea, Lanzarote, the Mars Desert Research Station and Mojave. Their climatology and daily series from 2020 to 2024 come from NASA POWER and Open-Meteo, elevation from Open Topo Data SRTM at 30 meters, place geometry from OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API, and lithology, soil and seismicity from Macrostrat, ISRIC SoilGrids and the USGS Earthquake Catalog.

Moon. The scientific base combines LRO LOLA elevation, declination, slope, roughness, Earth visibility and permanently shadowed regions, LRO Diviner thermal and polar resource products, LRO LROC mineralogy, crater inventories, lobate scarps, wrinkle ridges, swirls, impact melt ponds and pits, LRO Mini-RF circular polarization ratio, Lunar Prospector elemental abundances and magnetic data, SELENE mineralogy and nanophase iron, GRAIL gravity and crustal thickness, the Robbins crater database, Hiesinger mare ages and the USGS Unified Geologic Map of the Moon at 1:5,000,000. These yield 60 equal-area regions with 404 variables and 22,406 observation records, passing quality control with zero errors.

Mars. The scientific base combines MGS MOLA topography at 1/16 degree, MGS TES thermal inertia for day and night, Mars Odyssey GRS elemental and neutron data, MRO CRISM mineralogy for Jezero, the USGS global geologic map of Mars at 1:15,000,000, USGS SIM 3464 for Jezero and Nili Fossae, and Mars 2020 CTX orthomosaic, digital elevation model and slope at 5 and 20 meters, catalogued through NASA Mars Trek.

Reference target values. Seventy-seven target values across the eight bases, sixteen for the Moon and sixty-one for Mars, are recorded with unit, physical quantity, confidence level and source. Lunar thermal targets come from LRO Diviner, Martian atmospheric targets from Perseverance MEDA, Curiosity REMS and Phoenix MET, soil pH from Phoenix WCL, organic carbon from Curiosity SAM, cave skylights from Cushing et al. on Arsia Mons, and Shackleton illumination from NASA and LROC. Confidence is recorded as high for 31 values, medium for 18 and low for 28, and each target is tagged as a direct measurement, a classification defined by site geology, or a terrestrial equivalent where no comparable measurement exists.

Logistics and place names. One hundred and eighty-two support installations were compiled from NASA, ESA ESTRACK, JAXA, ILRS and IVS sources and public references. Region names come from OpenStreetMap Nominatim.

TECHNOLOGIES

Python for data engineering, modelling and the service layer. pandas and PyArrow with Parquet storage for 7.9 million Earth rows. Raster and vector geospatial processing over a global 0.5 degree grid and equal-area lunar regionalization. LightGBM for monthly environmental forecasting, tuned with Optuna. scikit-learn K-Means for clustering. A custom similarity ranking and recursive projection implementation for analog selection. FastAPI with Pydantic v2 for the read-only API. Angular 22, TypeScript and Three.js for the 3D application. pytest for testing, Ruff and mypy as quality gates, GitHub Actions for continuous integration.

METHODOLOGY

Comparable criteria. The taxonomy defines 21 niches, nine lunar and twelve Martian, expressed as 51 criteria over 34 distinct terrestrial variables. A variable can appear in more than one niche, so a single measurement can serve thermal and operational questions without duplicating data collection.

Real targets with relative tolerance. Each criterion compares a terrestrial value against a target taken from measurement. The criterion score is 100 minus 100 times the absolute deviation divided by the tolerance, floored at zero. Because many off-world targets lie far outside the terrestrial range, as with Martian pressure near 0.7 kilopascals or the lunar vacuum, each base carries its own tolerance per variable, defined as the largest distance between the target and the first and ninety-ninth percentiles of the Earth distribution. The nearest terrestrial location therefore scores highest and the rest fall proportionally, which keeps a meaningful gradient instead of collapsing every candidate to zero.

Coverage-aware aggregation. Criteria are combined by weighted mean, with weights renormalized over the criteria that are actually available. Admission requires overall coverage of at least 0.7 and per-niche coverage of at least 0.5, so a site is never rewarded or punished for data that does not exist. Strengths are labelled at 75 and above, weaknesses below 50.

Diversity. Clustering over 22 variables groups locations with similar environmental profiles, and selections enforce a 500 kilometer separation so that one desert cannot fill the entire shortlist. Classical analog sites and water-covered cells are excluded from automatic selection, which keeps the results focused on new candidates.

Logistics and cost-benefit. The logistic score is 0.4 times accessibility plus 0.35 times support plus 0.25 times routes. Accessibility decays exponentially with distance to the nearest United States installation at a 3,000 kilometer scale, support decays at 1,000 kilometers, and route availability counts installations within 2,500 kilometers with saturation at three. Cost-benefit is the square root of similarity times logistics, a deliberately compressive combination so that a high score on one axis cannot mask a low score on the other.

Focus and utility. A focus parameter sets the weight of logistics in the combined score: science uses zero, balanced uses 0.5, logistics uses one, producing a weighted geometric mean. Seven mission-oriented utility profiles re-average the niches that matter for a given campaign: habitat, mobility, geology, water and resources, astrobiology, extreme climate, and lava tubes.

Forecasting. Nine environmental variables are predicted one, two and three months ahead using LightGBM with Optuna hyperparameter search over 24 trials per series. Training runs through March 2026, validation covers April and May 2026, and test covers June, July and August 2026. Every model is compared against a persistence baseline, and the direct and recursive strategies follow Taieb and Hyndman, with climate context from the IPCC AR6 Atlas.

Explainability. Explanations are generated from the scores themselves, without external text. Each pair receives a narrative covering the reason it was selected, the niches that match with an example variable, the niches that differ with the most divergent variable, missing data, logistics and the forecast trend, plus short labels for interface display. A companion table exposes every variable's terrestrial value, target, tolerance, weight and score.

ARCHITECTURE

The pipeline is batch-oriented. Ingestion and ETL produce consolidated Parquet tables for Earth, Moon and Mars, which are normalized against the niche configuration. Three notebooks drive the analytical sequence: specification and clustering, monthly forecasting, and recommendation with mapping. Supporting modules implement scoring and coverage in analog_study, pairing and series generation in analog_pairs, logistics in logistics, forecasting in forecast_tuning, explanation text in explanations, and shared vocabulary in vocabulario. Outputs are materialized as Parquet artifacts under a single analog directory, which the API serves without recomputation.

The API is read-only and stateless. It exposes generic dataset discovery, records, filtering and aggregation over any table, model metadata, and a dedicated analog layer covering bases, sites, pairs, niche scores, cost-benefit rankings, support installations, filter vocabularies and recommendations. Every response carries a request identifier and a processing-time header, logs are structured, errors use a single envelope with controlled messages, and CORS origins are configuration-driven.

The application has three pages. A landing page introduces the project with planetary imagery. A methodology page presents the six comparison dimensions and the source-to-analog process. A map page renders Earth, Mars and the Moon as textured 3D bodies with site markers, a geodesic arc between targets and analogs, drag, zoom and body-switching controls, a detail panel for each site, and a filter panel for narrowing the displayed set.

IMPLEMENTED FUNCTIONALITY

Earth. 85,726 locations, 92 months, 7,886,792 rows, 16 dynamic and 67 static variables, with 12 MERRA-2 products and 4 MODIS products, plus population, natural events, lithology, soil, terrain and four derived variables.

Moon. 60 equal-area regions, 12 level-0 and 48 level-1, with 404 variables from 36 datasets and 22,406 observation records; quality control reports zero errors, six warnings and 537 informational flags.

Mars. Six reference bases with profiles built from MOLA, TES, Odyssey GRS, CRISM, USGS geologic maps and Mars 2020 CTX products.

Targets. 77 measured target values with source, unit, physical quantity and confidence, split into direct measurements, geological classifications and terrestrial equivalents.

Ranking. 358 pairs between eight bases and 187 terrestrial sites across 35 countries, split into 136 highlighted, 104 specialist, 61 cost-benefit and 57 general recommendations. Scores have a median of 66 and range from 29 to 81. Sixty-four pairs form the top cost-benefit set.

Niche and variable detail. 4,050 niche scores and 10,002 variable-level scores record how each pair performs criterion by criterion.

Series. 5,280 monthly rows covering September 2025 to November 2026, of which 4,224 are observed and 1,056 are forecast.

Logistics network. 182 support installations, 561 route records and 8 bases with position and display radius.

Forecasting. 27 variable-horizon series with 25 selected as LightGBM over the persistence baseline; two vegetative-index series were retained as insufficient-history references. Mean test error reduction is 41 percent, median 30.4 percent, ranging from 14.0 to 83.4 percent.

API. 18 GET routes: health, dataset listing and metadata, paginated records, single record, aggregations, model listing and metadata, and ten analog routes covering bases, base detail, sites, site detail, pairs, pair detail, niches, cost-benefit, filters and support installations, plus the recommendation endpoints for campaign-oriented queries.

Testing. 96 test functions across 12 modules, with continuous integration running Ruff, mypy and pytest on every push and pull request.

RESULTS

The platform produces a complete analog ranking for two lunar and six Martian bases, with a logistics view, a forecasting view and a per-variable audit trail for every recommendation.

The reported top analogs are internally consistent with the underlying criteria. The lunar south pole base resolves to Antarctic and Greenland ice-sheet margins and to Nunavut, matching polar illumination and thermal extremes. The lunar mare tube base resolves to the Gobi region of Mongolia, the Jufra region of Libya and New Mexico, matching basaltic terrain and subsurface potential. Jezero resolves to the Hormozgan province of Iran and to Red Sea coastal desert in Sudan and Egypt, matching clay mineralogy and arid exposure. Gale resolves to Kandahar in Afghanistan, South Khorasan in Iran and Beni Abbes in Algeria. Meridiani resolves to Xinjiang in China and to the Sirte and Butnan regions of Libya. The mid-latitude Mars base resolves to Antarctic interior sites, as expected from its thermal and illumination profile. The Tharsis tube region resolves to Xinjiang, Tibesti in Chad and Isfahan in Iran. The Medusae Fossae yardang field resolves to Kandahar, Beni Abbes and Tabuk in Saudi Arabia, matching strong aeolian regimes and dust exposure.

Forecasting outperforms the persistence baseline consistently, with a mean error reduction of 41 percent across 25 series and gains above 14 percent in the weakest case, indicating a stable predictive signal rather than tuning noise.

Every published figure is reproducible from committed artifacts at a known commit, and every score is decomposable down to the individual variable, its target, its tolerance, its weight and its source.

TEAM

Guilherme Teixeira: 33 commits including 16 merges. Integration and merge stewardship, repository-wide coordination, notebook work and dataset regeneration.

Jose Roberio: 12 commits including 3 merges. Real target values, analog explanations, API filters, schema and service work.

Luis Rodrigues: 7 commits including 1 merge. Front-end application, including the landing page, the methodology page, the 3D map, the filter panel and the visual assets.

Henrique Rodrigues: 4 commits. Focused component contributions.

Bruno: 3 commits. Additional component contributions.

Helena Neves: 2 commits including 1 merge. Documentation and supporting changes.

CREDITS AND LICENSES

All planetary and Earth-observation datasets used in this project are provided by NASA and are in the public domain. Credit is given to the missions, instruments, science teams and archives that produced them.

Earth observations: NASA GIBS and the MERRA-2 reanalysis, covering air temperature, precipitation, snowfall, evaporation, root-zone soil water, precipitable water vapour, incident shortwave radiation, albedo, wind speed, dust concentration, dust deposition and aerosol optical depth; MODIS Terra for daytime and nighttime land surface temperature, NDVI and IGBP land cover; NASA SEDAC GPW v4 population density; NASA EONET natural events; NASA POWER climatology and daily series; and NASA Earth imagery used for the globe texture.

Moon: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA, for elevation, declination, slope, roughness, Earth visibility and permanently shadowed regions; LRO Diviner global cumulative and polar resource products; LRO LROC, for mineralogy, craters, lobate scarps, wrinkle ridges, swirls, impact melt ponds and pits; LRO Mini-RF circular polarization ratio; Lunar Prospector GRS elemental abundances and magnetometer data; GRAIL gravity and crustal thickness; the Robbins lunar crater database; Hiesinger mare ages; the USGS Unified Geologic Map of the Moon at 1:5,000,000; and NASA lunar imagery used for the globe texture.

Mars: Mars Global Surveyor MOLA topography and TES thermal inertia; Mars Odyssey GRS elemental and neutron data; Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CRISM mineralogy; the USGS global geologic map of Mars at 1:15,000,000 and USGS SIM 3464 for Jezero and Nili Fossae; Mars 2020 CTX orthomosaic, digital elevation model and slope; the NASA Mars Trek catalogue; and NASA Martian imagery used for the globe texture.

Reference measurements: NASA Moon and Mars Fact Sheets; LRO Diviner thermal measurements after Williams et al.; Perseverance MEDA after Rodriguez-Manfredi et al.; Curiosity REMS after Gomez-Elvira et al.; Curiosity SAM organic carbon after Stern et al.; Phoenix MET pressure and temperature; Phoenix WCL soil pH after Hecht et al.; Arsia Mons cave skylights after Cushing et al.; and NASA and LROC illumination studies for Shackleton.

Base coordinates and site identification: NASA mission pages.

Logistics catalogue: 182 support installations compiled from NASA, ESA ESTRACK, JAXA, ILRS and IVS sources.

Supplementary open data, used under their respective licenses: USGS Astrogeology products and the USGS Earthquake Catalog, public domain; OpenStreetMap, including the Overpass API and Nominatim geocoding, under the Open Database License, with attribution to OpenStreetMap contributors; Macrostrat, CC-BY 4.0; ISRIC SoilGrids 2.0, CC-BY 4.0; Open-Meteo, CC-BY 4.0; Open Topo Data SRTM at 30 meters; AWS Terrain Tiles derived from SRTM, ETOPO1 and GMTED; SELENE and Kaguya products, with attribution to JAXA and the original investigators.

Methodological references: Taieb and Hyndman on direct and recursive forecasting strategies; the IPCC AR6 Atlas for climate context; Wieczorek et al. for GRAIL crustal thickness.

Challenge marks: the NASA and Space Apps logos are used to identify the challenge context.

NEXT STEPS

Continue extending the reference target set with additional measured values and confidence grading, so that more criteria move from terrestrial equivalents to direct measurements.

Publish sensitivity analyses showing how rankings respond to changes in tolerance, weighting and target confidence.

Extend forecasting beyond three months and add calibrated prediction intervals to the point forecasts.

Expand the application from curated reference sites to full catalog exploration, with layered terrain, geology and seasonal views.

Add an optional authenticated tier, rate limiting and pagination for programmatic partners as query volume grows.

Package a single end-to-end command that regenerates every artifact from raw sources, together with a pinned environment specification.
